41499:
In the Hebrew Bible Daniel is placed among the Writings (*Ketuvim*), not the Prophets. The Talmud reflects this, distinguishing Daniel from the prophets Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi (Megillah 3a). Some explain the placement by the book's late date, others by its genre, or by the view that Daniel was a wise man to whom God revealed things rather than a prophet sent to Israel. Daniel is not read as a haftarah in the synagogue, but its heroes are honoured as models of *kiddush ha-Shem*, sanctifying God's name by being ready to die rather than worship idols. Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah (Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego) are remembered in the Talmud and liturgy alongside other martyrs.

The book is closely tied to Hanukkah. The persecution under Antiochus IV and the 'abomination of desolation' (Dan 11:31; Dan 12:11) are the events from which the Maccabees rescued the temple. 1 Maccabees uses Daniel's language of 'the desolating sacrilege', and Mattathias' farewell speech cites Daniel and his friends as models (according to 1 Macc 2:59-60).

Rabbinic interpreters often read Daniel's visions messianically, but carefully. The Talmud warns against calculating the end (Sanhedrin 97b), even as some sages explored Daniel's numbers. Rashi read the seventy weeks of Dan 9 as ending with the Roman destruction of the second temple in AD 70. The 'one like a son of man' coming with the clouds (Dan 7:13) was read both as the Messiah (Sanhedrin 98a contrasts his coming 'with the clouds' and 'lowly, riding on a donkey', Zech 9:9) and, as Dan 7:18 and Dan 7:27 suggest, as a symbol of 'the holy ones of the Most High', faithful Israel. Covenantally, Daniel's prayer in chapter 9 is a model: he confesses Israel's sin, appeals to God's covenant faithfulness and to his name, and asks God to act 'for your own sake' (Dan 9:4-19).
41501: Four young exiles refuse the king's food and are blessed with wisdom.
41503: Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a statue smashed by a stone that becomes a mountain: God's everlasting kingdom.
41505: Three friends refuse to bow and are rescued in the fire; Nebuchadnezzar goes mad until he acknowledges the Most High.
41506: Writing on the wall and lions
41507: Belshazzar profanes temple vessels and loses his kingdom that night; Daniel prays despite a decree and is saved from the lions.
41508: Beasts and the son of man
41509: Four beasts rise from the sea; the Ancient of Days gives everlasting dominion to one like a son of man and the holy ones.
41511: Persia and Greece clash; a little horn desecrates the sanctuary; Daniel's confession brings the seventy-weeks revelation.
41513: An angel recounts centuries of conflict ending with a blasphemous king and a time of distress.
41515: Michael arises, the dead awake to life or shame, the wise shine like stars, and Daniel is told to rest until the end.
41537: Kingdom, kingship, reign; the book's central theme, used dozens of times for human empires and God's everlasting reign.
41538: 'A human being'. In contrast to the beasts, a human figure comes with the clouds, the way God himself travels in the Old Testament, and receives eternal dominion.
41539: A secret or hidden plan revealed by God, a word borrowed from Persian. It appears in the Dead Sea Scrolls and lies behind Paul's 'mystery'.
41541: Holy ones or saints. In Dan 7 it may mean faithful Israel, angels, or both, who receive the kingdom.
41543: Those who have insight and teach many; they will suffer but will shine like stars.
41544: Daniel at Nebuchadnezzar's court mirrors Joseph at Pharaoh's: a young exile interprets a king's dream when the experts fail and is promoted.
41545: Daniel reads Jeremiah's prophecy of seventy years and prays for its fulfilment.
41546: Both are stories of Jews in foreign courts facing deadly decrees, showing faithful life in the diaspora.
41547: Jesus warns of 'the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel' and claims the son of man's coming with the clouds before the high priest.
41548: Revelation draws heavily on Daniel: the son of man, beasts from the sea, time-times-and-half, and books opened in judgment.
41549: Hebrews alludes to those who 'shut the mouths of lions' and 'quenched the power of fire' as heroes of faith.
41550: 'Son of Man' was Jesus' favourite way of referring to himself, and at his trial he joined Dan 7:13 to Ps 110:1: 'you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven' (Mark 14:62), a claim the high priest heard as blasphemy. Jesus' proclamation of 'the kingdom of God' takes up Daniel's promise of a kingdom God would set up that would never be destroyed (Dan 2:44; Mark 1:15). Revelation pictures the risen Jesus with features of both the son of man and the Ancient of Days (Rev 1:13-14; Dan 7:9). Many Christians have read the seventy weeks (Dan 9:24-27) as pointing to the time of the Messiah's coming and death. Jewish interpreters read the son of man as the Messiah or as Israel, and the seventy weeks as ending in the second-temple period, but do not identify the Messiah with Jesus. Critical scholars often read the original son of man as the archangel Michael or as a symbol of faithful Israel vindicated.
41551: The seventieth week as a future seven-year tribulation
41552: Dan 9:27 predicts that a future Antichrist will make a seven-year peace treaty with Israel, break it halfway, and set up an abomination in a rebuilt temple; there is a long gap (the church age) between the 69th and 70th weeks.
41553: The 'gap' and future Antichrist reading developed mainly in 19th-century dispensationalism (J. N. Darby, later the Scofield Bible). Other readings are older and widely held: the seventy weeks end with Antiochus IV in 167-164 BC (most critical scholars, e.g. John Collins); or they culminate in the Messiah's death and the temple's destruction in AD 70 (many early church writers, Reformed and other evangelical scholars). The numbers are probably symbolic (ten jubilee cycles of seven times seven years). Scholars such as Ernest Lucas and Tremper Longman note how differently the details can be calculated.
41554: Dispensational scholars such as John Walvoord, Harold Hoehner (who calculated the 69 weeks precisely to AD 33) and Stephen Miller defend the future-week view, arguing that the six goals of Dan 9:24 are not yet fully accomplished and that Jesus placed the 'abomination' in the future (Matt 24:15). This is a genuine debate among evangelicals, not simply a popular mistake.
41555: Which reading one holds shapes views of Israel, the end times and current events. Knowing that faithful scholars disagree guards against treating one end-times chart as essential to the gospel.
41557: Daniel's vegetables-and-water diet is a biblical model for healthy eating or a spiritual 'Daniel Fast' that guarantees health and breakthroughs.
41558: Daniel's concern was loyalty, not nutrition. Eating the king's food would mark him as the king's dependant and perhaps involve unclean or idol-offered food (Dan 1:8). The point of the ten-day test is that God, not the king's rich table, gave them health and wisdom (Dan 1:17). Later Daniel eats normally and fasts from meat and wine only during a period of mourning (Dan 10:2-3). Commentators across traditions (Goldingay, Longman, Lucas) agree.
41559: Many evangelical teachers who promote the 'Daniel Fast' present it as a voluntary spiritual discipline inspired by the text, not as a command or guarantee, which is reasonable. The concern is only when it is taught as the meaning of Dan 1.
41560: The real lesson is how to serve faithfully inside a powerful system without being owned by it, a question for every believer in work and public life.
41561: Daniel taught Jews under pagan empires, from Babylon to Antiochus IV, that God still ruled, that faithfulness was worth dying for, and that God would vindicate the faithful, even beyond death.
41562: Daniel helps believers serve faithfully in secular institutions, resist the pull of powers that demand ultimate loyalty, pray with confession and hope, and trust that all empires are temporary while God's kingdom endures.
41563: A prophet's broken marriage becomes a living picture of God's wounded, stubborn love for an Israel that keeps running to other lovers.
41565: The only writing prophet who was a native of the northern kingdom. He speaks of Israel's land, shrines and kings from the inside, calling the nation 'Ephraim' and its capital 'Samaria'. Nothing is known of his trade or town; what we know is his marriage to Gomer and the names of his three children.
41566: The heading names him and dates him by kings of both Judah and Israel (Hos 1:1). The northern vocabulary and the unusual, difficult Hebrew fit a northern speaker. Most scholars think his oracles were carried south to Judah after Samaria fell in 722 BC and edited there, which explains the Judean kings in the heading and several lines about Judah.
41567: Northern kingdom of Israel (Samaria region); edited later in Judah
41568: Hosea spoke in the north. The book as we have it was probably collected and finished in Jerusalem by people who saw his warnings come true.
41569: The people, priests and royal house of the northern kingdom ('Ephraim')
41570: Samaria, Bethel ('Beth-aven'), Gilgal and the northern shrines
41571: A nation sliding from wealth under Jeroboam II into chaos: four of its last six kings were assassinated, rival parties courted Assyria and Egypt by turns, and worship of the LORD had blended with Baal fertility rites.
41572: Death of Jeroboam II; his son Zechariah is murdered after six months, beginning a run of coups in Israel.
41573: Tiglath-pileser III takes the Assyrian throne and turns Assyria into a standing empire that annexes conquered lands.
41574: Menahem of Israel pays heavy tribute to Assyria (2 Kgs 15:19-20).
41575: Syro-Ephraimite war: Israel and Damascus attack Judah; Assyria responds and strips Israel of Galilee and Gilead.
41576: Samaria falls to Assyria after a three-year siege; the northern kingdom ends and many are deported.
41577:
Hosea began preaching in the last good years of Jeroboam II, when Israel was rich, its borders wide and its shrines busy. Within a few years everything came apart. Kings were murdered in quick succession (Zechariah, Shallum, Pekahiah and Pekah all died by violence), and each faction had a foreign policy: pay off Assyria, or look to Egypt for help. Hosea compares Israel to 'a silly dove' flying back and forth between the two powers (Hos 7:11) and says the people made kings 'but not by me' (Hos 8:4).

Religiously, the problem was not that Israel had forgotten the LORD's name but that they worshipped him as if he were Baal, the Canaanite storm god who was believed to send rain and fertility. Sacrifices on the hilltops, sacred prostitution or sexual rites, and calf images at Bethel and Dan mixed the LORD with the local gods. People still went to the festivals, but they thought grain, wine and oil came from Baal (Hos 2:5-8).

Assyria under Tiglath-pileser III was no longer a raider but an empire that deported whole populations and resettled them. Hosea's warnings of exile were not abstract: he lived to see Galilee and Gilead stripped away in 733-732 BC, and his book carries the shadow of Samaria's fall in 722 BC.
41579: Hosea pictures the covenant between the LORD and Israel as a marriage: the LORD is the husband who rescued and provided, Israel the bride who chased other 'lovers'. Idolatry is not merely bad theology but adultery, a betrayal of a relationship.
41580: Baal ('lord', 'master', 'husband') was the Canaanite god of storm and fertility. Hosea plays on the word: one day Israel will call God 'my husband' (ishi), no longer 'my Baal' (baali).
41582: Children's names carried messages. Jezreel recalls Jehu's massacre at Jezreel; Lo-ruhamah means 'not pitied'; Lo-ammi means 'not my people', an undoing of the covenant formula 'you are my people'. Later the names are reversed.
41584: A rib is a legal case. The LORD brings charges against his people as in a court, listing the broken terms of the covenant: no faithfulness, no loyal love, no knowledge of God.
41586: In Hebrew, 'to know' (yada) includes intimacy and loyalty, not just information. It is used of husband and wife. Israel's 'lack of knowledge' is a relationship gone cold, and the priests are blamed for it.
41588: Alongside the marriage picture, Hosea uses the parent image: God taught Ephraim to walk and lifted him to his cheek. Exodus is remembered as adoption.
41589:
Hosea opens the Twelve (Trei Asar), which Jewish tradition treats as a single book on one scroll; Ben Sira already speaks of 'the twelve prophets' around 180 BC, and the Talmud (*Bava Batra* 14b) explains that the short prophecies were joined so that none would be lost. For a Jewish reader Hosea is above all a book about teshuvah (returning). Its closing chapter, 'Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God' (Hos 14:1-2), opens the haftarah for Shabbat Shuvah, the 'Sabbath of Return' between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. Its line 'take with you words' (Hos 14:2) was read by the rabbis as a charter for prayer standing in place of sacrifice once the temple was gone. Hosea 6:6, 'I desired mercy (hesed) and not sacrifice', was similarly used after AD 70: a well-known story in *Avot de-Rabbi Natan* has Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai comfort a disciple at the temple ruins by saying that acts of loving-kindness now atone.

The marriage image lives in daily practice. When a Jewish man winds the tefillin strap around his finger each weekday morning he recites Hosea 2:19-20 (Hebrew 2:21-22), 'I will betroth you to me forever... in faithfulness, and you shall know the LORD.' The covenant is renewed as a betrothal, every day. Hosea 2 is also the haftarah for Bamidbar, read near Shavuot, the festival of the Sinai covenant, so the wilderness 'honeymoon' (Hos 2:14-15) is heard alongside Israel's wilderness journey.

The Talmud (*Pesahim* 87a-b) tells a pointed story: when God told Hosea that Israel had sinned, Hosea answered 'exchange them for another nation'. God then had him marry Gomer, and when Hosea could not bear to send away his own wife and children, God said, in effect, 'Neither can I abandon mine.' Medieval interpreters disagreed on whether the marriage was a real event (Rashi tends to read it narratively) or a prophetic vision (Ibn Ezra and Maimonides). Either way, the relationship, not the transaction, is the heart of the book: God is hurt, argues with himself, and refuses to let go (Hos 11:8-9).
41591: God tells Hosea to marry Gomer, and the children's names announce judgment on the house of Jehu and the covenant itself.
41593: The LORD pleads with unfaithful Israel, strips away Baal's 'gifts', then woos her back in the wilderness and betroths her forever.
41595: Hosea pays to redeem his wife and sets a waiting period, a picture of exile followed by return to 'David their king'.
41597: Priests, kings and people are indicted for cult prostitution, calf worship, coups and foreign alliances; shallow repentance is exposed.
41599: Jacob's story, the exodus and the wilderness are retold to show a long pattern of ingratitude; exile 'back to Egypt' looms.
41601: The LORD cannot give Ephraim up: 'I am God and not a man.' Love overrules the logic of punishment.
41603: A model prayer of repentance and God's promise to heal and love freely; the wise will understand these ways.
41604: Hosea: love that will not let go
41625: Loyal, committed covenant love: kindness that keeps its promises. God wants it more than sacrifice, and Israel's version of it is 'like the morning dew' that vanishes.
41626: To turn around and come back; the basic Hebrew word for repentance. Hosea uses it both for Israel's return to God and for God turning from anger.
41628: Intimate, loyal acquaintance with God, shown in obeying and trusting him; its absence is the root charge against Israel.
41630: To be sexually unfaithful; used for Israel's chasing of other gods and allies. It stresses betrayal within a relationship.
41631: Hosea's charges follow Deuteronomy's covenant terms and its curses (no rain, exile), and his call to love and know God echoes Deuteronomy's 'love the LORD your God'.
41632: Jeremiah takes up Hosea's marriage metaphor for Judah a century later, including the wilderness honeymoon and the divorced wife invited back.
41633: Ezekiel extends the marriage allegory into a long, graphic history of Jerusalem's unfaithfulness and God's everlasting covenant.
41634: Matthew applies 'out of Egypt I called my son' to Jesus, who relives Israel's story, and Jesus twice quotes 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice'.
41635: Paul uses the reversal of Lo-ammi ('not my people' becomes 'my people') to describe God calling Gentiles as well as Jews.
41636: Paul's taunt 'O death, where is your sting?' draws on Hosea's question to death and the grave.
41637: Christians read Hosea's redeeming of Gomer as a picture of God's costly love that buys back the unfaithful, fulfilled in Christ who 'loved the church and gave himself for her' (Eph 5:25). Matthew sees Jesus as the true 'son' called out of Egypt (Matt 2:15), the one who succeeds where Israel failed. Jesus himself uses Hosea 6:6 to defend eating with sinners and to rebuke rigid Sabbath rules (Matt 9:13; Matt 12:7). The 'third day' raising in Hosea 6:2 is often linked by Christians to the resurrection, though the NT never quotes it directly. Jewish readers, for their part, hear Hosea as a promise to Israel itself: the same people who were called 'not my people' will again be 'children of the living God' (Hos 1:10). Both readings agree the book is about God's refusal to abandon his covenant partner.
41638: 'My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge' (Hos 4:6)
41639: This verse is often preached as a call to study more, get informed, learn Bible doctrine or even get educated generally: Christians suffer because they do not know enough facts.
41640: In Hosea 'knowledge of God' is relational: loyalty, obedience and intimacy, the opposite of adultery (Hos 2:20; Hos 6:6). The charge in Hos 4:4-9 is aimed at the priests, who were supposed to teach Torah and instead profited from the people's sin offerings. Hans Walter Wolff and Andersen & Freedman stress that 'knowledge' here means the priestly teaching of the covenant and the living relationship it was meant to sustain.
41641: Evangelical commentators such as Douglas Stuart and Derek Kidner agree the knowledge is covenantal, not merely intellectual, but point out that it includes real content: Torah taught and remembered. So the popular use is not entirely wrong; teaching matters. It is narrowed when it loses the relational point and the warning to religious leaders.
41642: Read in context, the verse is a warning to leaders who feed on people's failures and a call to a loyal relationship with God, not simply a motivation for more information.
41644: Popular devotional reading treats Hosea 2 simply as a romance: God the faithful lover pursuing his wayward bride, a picture of grace to each believer.
41645: Feminist scholars such as Renita Weems and Gale Yee note that the chapter also uses images of stripping and exposing the wife (Hos 2:3; Hos 2:10). They warn that, read literally as a model for human marriage, it can seem to excuse a husband's abuse. They read it as a metaphor shaped by an ancient patriarchal culture, describing a nation's collapse under war and exile.
41646: Traditional and evangelical scholars (e.g. Douglas Stuart, Duane Garrett) agree the passage is metaphor for national judgment, drawn from the covenant curses (Deut 28), not a guide to how husbands should treat wives. They stress that the chapter ends in tender wooing, not violence, and that God's goal is restoration. Both sides agree it must not be used to justify abuse.
41647: Seeing both the shock and the tenderness keeps readers from sentimentalising judgment or misusing the text in real marriages.
41648: For Israel the message was: your crisis is not mainly political but relational. Kings, treaties and harvest rituals will not save you; only returning to the God who loves you will. When Samaria fell, the book explained why, and its promises gave refugees reason to hope.
41649: Hosea speaks to anyone who treats God as a supplier of blessings rather than a partner in love. It asks what we credit for our 'grain, wine and oil', and what we run to under pressure. It also gives one of the Bible's most moving pictures of a God who feels, grieves and refuses to give up on people who have betrayed him.
41650: A locust plague becomes a warning of the Day of the LORD, and a call to return with all the heart is answered by God's promise to pour out his Spirit on everyone.
41651: A Judean prophet, otherwise unknown. His close interest in the temple, its offerings and its priests has led some to think he was a temple ('cultic') prophet, though that is a guess.
41652: Only the heading names him (Joel 1:1). His era must be worked out from clues inside the book, which is why dates range over four centuries.
41653: The book assumes a working temple, priests 'between the porch and the altar' and the city walls (Joel 2:9; Joel 2:17).
41654: The people, elders and priests of Judah
41655: Swarms of locusts and drought have stripped vines, fig trees and grain; there is nothing left to offer at the temple. Joel calls a national fast and reads the disaster as a preview of a greater day of judgment.
41656: Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the first temple; Judah's people are scattered (an event Joel 3:1-3 may look back on).
41657: The second temple is completed under Persian rule.
41658: Nehemiah rebuilds Jerusalem's walls (on the Persian-period dating, Joel's 'wall' would be this one).
41659: Greek and Phoenician traders are active in the eastern Mediterranean slave trade (compare Joel 3:4-6).
